sup-a42fb5d36ded05c7-q1:whole.hint: Mark the potential difference across the component and the current through it. Are these the quantities given?
notes: For a resistor, V = IR. Series components carry the same current; parallel branches have the same potential difference.
Simplify a resistor network from the innermost series or parallel combination outwards. Resistances add in series; conductances 1/R add in parallel.

sup-a42fb5d36ded05c7-q2:whole.hint: Consider both the wire’s length and its cross-sectional area, especially if it is stretched.
notes: Resistance R = ρL/A. For a circular wire A = πd²/4, so changing diameter affects resistance quadratically.
If volume is conserved during stretching, increasing length also reduces area. Resistivity is a material property at a stated temperature, not the same as resistance.

sup-a42fb5d36ded05c7-q4:whole.hint: Distinguish the energy supplied per coulomb by the source from the voltage available across its terminals.
notes: For a discharging cell, ε = I(R + r) and terminal voltage V = ε − Ir. Internal resistance dissipates some of the source’s power.
A graph of terminal V against I has intercept ε and gradient −r. Check whether the cell is delivering or receiving current before using the voltage sign.

sup-a42fb5d36ded05c7-q5:whole.hint: Check which axis is voltage and which is current; the gradient depends on that choice.
notes: For an ohmic component, the V–I gradient is resistance and the I–V gradient is conductance. For a non-ohmic component, the operating-point ratio V/I is not generally the local gradient.
Read the operating voltage and current from the same point. A curve through the origin need not represent constant resistance.
